name.text: Chain Rule Application for Computing a Derivative

questiontext.text:
Given the following information

\( \displaystyle w= {@func_w@}\)

\(\displaystyle x={@func_x@}\)

\(\displaystyle y={@func_y@}\)

\(\displaystyle z={@func_z@}\)

Use Chain Rule to compute \(\displaystyle \frac{dw}{dt}\)

\(\displaystyle \frac{dw}{dt} = \) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution


From this information it looks like the chain rule for this case should be,

\( \displaystyle \frac{dw}{dt}= \frac{\partial{w}}{\partial{x}}\frac{d{x}}{d{t}}+\frac{\partial{w}}{\partial{y}}\frac{d{y}}{d{t}}+\frac{\partial{w}}{\partial{z}}\frac{d{z}}{d{t}} \)

\(\displaystyle \quad= {@func1a@}({@func1b@})+{@func2a@}({@func2b@})+{@func3a@}({@func3b@}) \)

\( \quad= {@ta@}\)

truefeedback.text:
You seem to have computed the derivative of the function \( w \) alone without factoring in the other functions \( x,y &, z\) in your computation.

Hint:

\( \displaystyle \frac{dw}{dt}= \frac{\partial{w}}{\partial{x}}\frac{d{x}}{d{t}}+\frac{\partial{w}}{\partial{y}}\frac{d{y}}{d{t}}+\frac{\partial{w}}{\partial{z}}\frac{d{z}}{d{t}} \)

You seem to have computed the derivative of all the three functions wrt to t and added the result.

Hint:

Suppose we have three functions as shown,

\( z=f(x,y), x=g(t), y=h(t),\)

in order to compute \( \displaystyle \frac{dz}{dt}\), you’ll have to compute an ordinary derivative since \(z\) really would be a function of \(t\) only if we were to substitute in for \(x\) and \(y\).

Thus, the chain rule for this case is,

\( \displaystyle \frac{dz}{dt}= \frac{\partial{z}}{\partial{x}}\frac{d{x}}{d{t}}+\frac{\partial{z}}{\partial{y}}\frac{d{y}}{d{t}}\)
